summary: Defines a SIP event package for session-specific policies. It lets user agents subscribe to the policies for a SIP session and get notifications if those policies change. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like signing up for text alerts about house rules. If the rules for your call change, you are told.

questions: sip event package for session policies
how to subscribe to sip session policy changes
subtitle: The SIP subscription that lets a phone ask a policy server what is allowed for its call and hear about changes.

tldr.problem: A SIP user agent needs a standard way to send a policy server the details of a session and to receive the resulting rules, including later changes.
tldr.mechanism: It defines the event package session-spec-policy: the user agent sends a SUBSCRIBE whose body describes the session, and the policy server answers and updates with NOTIFY requests that carry the policy decision.
tldr.outcome: This is the policy channel used by the session policy framework. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No more than once every five seconds

today: RFC 6795 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and RFC 6794 requires user agents to support it as the policy channel for SIP and SIPS policy server URIs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The session policy framework in RFC 6794 lets a proxy define and influence policies on sessions, such as the codecs or media types to be used, and it helps user agents find the URIs of session-specific policy servers. This RFC supplies the missing piece: a SIP event package, built on RFC 6665, with which a user agent subscribes to session-specific policies on a policy server.

The subscriber submits the details of its intended session, for example audio and video, in the body of a SUBSCRIBE request and asks whether it is permissible. The policy server (the notifier) answers with a decision: deny, propose changes, or accept as proposed. An example is disallowing video while agreeing to the rest. The first decision goes in a NOTIFY, and later changes, such as a change in available bandwidth, go in further NOTIFY requests.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the rule keeper your plan. They say yes, no, or yes if you change one thing, and they tell you again if the answer changes.

sections.title: The Event Package Definition
sections.content:
The package name is session-spec-policy. It defines two optional parameters that exist only in NOTIFY requests and MUST be ignored in a SUBSCRIBE:

  • local-only says the notifier does not need the remote session description.
  • insufficient-info says a policy decision could not be made because the subscriber did not provide enough information.

The default subscription duration is two hours. Because a subscription lives about as long as the session, the exact value matters little but SHOULD be longer than a typical session. The notifier may end the subscription early, for instance if the policies will not change. The subscriber MUST NOT end it unless the session is ending or the notifier is no longer in the list of relevant policy servers, and it MUST refresh it before it expires. Notifications SHOULD NOT be generated more often than once every five seconds, and the rate of policy change is expected to be very low.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-up has a name, two special flags that mean 'I do not need to see the other side' and 'you did not tell me enough', and it lasts two hours unless renewed.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY Bodies
sections.content:
A SUBSCRIBE MUST carry a body that describes a SIP session, because the Request-URI, package name and parameters do not identify what the subscription is about. All subscribers and notifiers MUST support the MIME type application/media-policy-dataset+xml from RFC 6796, which is the default. Other formats may be negotiated. The RFC prefers this format over raw SDP because it can hold information SDP cannot (for example the target URI), it carries local and remote descriptions in one document, and it matches the format used for session-independent policies. The cost is that the user agent must encode session information in that format.

The NOTIFY body holds the policy. If the SUBSCRIBE contained only the local session description, the NOTIFY MUST hold a policy for it. If it contained local and remote descriptions, the NOTIFY MUST hold two policies. Each policy document MUST be a complete decision. Deltas and partial decisions are not supported. The Accept header field defaults to the media policy type.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-up form describes your call, and the reply is a full answer sheet, never just 'the same as before except one thing'.

sections.title: Subscriber and Notifier Behavior
sections.content:
The subscriber MUST describe the session as fully as it can and use its most recent session description. With an offer/answer exchange it MUST include the local description, such as its offer. It SHOULD also include the remote description when it has one, unless it has seen the local-only parameter. If it has no description yet, for instance when sending an empty INVITE, it SHOULD still subscribe and MUST refresh the subscription once the description exists. It MUST also refresh whenever the session description changes. If the server fails, the subscriber SHOULD look for an alternative server, and MAY continue the session without policies if none is found, though enforcement may then block it.

The notifier SHOULD authenticate and authorize subscriptions and MUST respond quickly, because the subscription may be created between receiving a 200 OK and sending the ACK, and a slow first NOTIFY delays the ACK. If it lacks information it SHOULD accept the subscription and send a NOTIFY with insufficient-info. It MAY notify at any time, typically when the decision changes, for example when the network gets congested or a session moves from business hours into evening hours. It SHOULD end the subscription when it rejects a session for good, and keep it alive when it expects to admit the session soon.

The subscriber MUST apply each decision. If it will not, it MUST NOT set up the session, MUST end it if it is running, and MUST cancel or reject a pending INVITE. A rejected session should not be retried unchanged. A later update that requires changes may need a re-INVITE or UPDATE, or may end the session, for example when the account runs out of credit or an emergency requires ending non-emergency calls.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the rule keeper as much as you can and update them if your plan changes. They answer quickly, and you must follow the answer or call it off.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content: The informative example in the RFC shows Alice's phone setting up a call to Bob with a policy server already known. Alice first sends a SUBSCRIBE with Event: session-spec-policy and Expires: 7200 to a SIPS URI, with her offer in the body. The server replies 200 OK and sends a NOTIFY with a policy for the offer. Alice then sends the INVITE to Bob, receives his 200 OK and sends the ACK. She then refreshes the subscription with her offer and Bob's answer, and the server sends a NOTIFY with a policy for each. The RFC states that these flows are informative and not normative.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice checks the rules for her offer first, then calls Bob, then checks the rules again now that she knows what Bob agreed to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Policies can change what a user agent does, so an attacker could use them to harm it, for example by setting available bandwidth to zero to end a session. The session information sent to the server can be sensitive, even containing media encryption keys, and the policies can reveal network details or service level agreements.

Policy servers SHOULD be addressable only through a SIPS URI, and both sides MUST support TLS. The user agent SHOULD check that the identity in the server's X.509 certificate matches the policy server URI. The server SHOULD authenticate a new subscription using a certificate or HTTP Digest, and MAY give a generic policy to a user agent it cannot authenticate. S/MIME MAY be used for end-to-end integrity, with a caution quoted from RFC 3261 that some intermediaries need to see SDP. Finally, even over a secure session, the user agent should not send sensitive data like session keys, and the server should not send data the user agent has no need for.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a locked line, check who you are talking to, and do not hand over secrets the other side does not need.
